title: Legal data: Connected records enable operational transformation
desc: Advocates selective data preparation linking workload, business context and workflow while preserving judgment, access controls and security.

kps.k: The central proposition is that AI-enabled legal transformation depends on turning fragmented records into usable operational and business information, not simply adding tools.
kps.d: The contributions frame legal data as a resource for managing demand, anticipating risk, improving decisions and demonstrating value. Darr describes integrating DHL’s intake, matter, spend and business data into dashboards; Smolik reports hiring data expertise to organise and interpret it. These accounts describe the same organisational setting, not independent demonstrations of effectiveness. McIver warns that AI exposes scattered, poor-quality data, while Saunders identifies the burden of separating useful information from redundant, obsolete and trivial material. The evidence chiefly comprises practitioner accounts and product descriptions, rather than measured causal effects.

qs.q: Um and then on top of that we have spent a lot of time and hiring analysts on our team to actually take all the data that's available in those underlying applications and and pull it together with some of the business applications to have a full suite of reporting.
qs.a: Elaine Darr — DHL Supply Chain (VP Legal & Regulatory Affairs) on legal ops, trained models, and market-rate billing enforcement · In-house counsel · 2025

qs.q: Now that we do have the data organized in a way, you got to have somebody to interpret it.

kps.k: Data preparation should be selective and workflows must tolerate imperfect inputs.
kps.d: The main qualification concerns how much standardisation organisations can realistically achieve. Greg Lambert, with Nuara’s agreement, warns that automation can amplify messy processes and data. McIver and the speaker in Legal Marketing, AI, Innovation, and Why People Still Come First recommend prioritising useful fields and cleaning tasks rather than preparing everything. Skoghag explicitly qualifies the standardisation argument: firms can organise their own systems but cannot impose identical metadata practices on clients. The practical implication is to choose data around a defined use case and build procurement and workflows for variable formats and readability, rather than assume ideal inputs.

qs.q: if if you start with a messy processes and data, you’re going to amplify that messy process and that messy data rather than clean it up.
qs.a: Flatiron Law Group's Lennie Nuara on Talent-First AI, M&A Workflows, and the Future of Legal Practice · Law firms · 2026

qs.q: And a lot of times it’s not needing all of the data that you have and it’s going back and saying, let’s get this a little bit more simplistic.
qs.a: Data First, Partner Better. Jennifer McIver on Legal Ops Benchmarks, AI Agents, and Pricing Reality Checks · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Legal departments need to connect workload visibility with business context, staffing and workflow design.
kps.d: Darr wants historical demand to inform headcount and skills, while Smolik proposes using past experience to anticipate business risks, conditional on those patterns recurring. McNairn emphasises coordinating all legal work rather than merely storing contracts, and Fleisher argues that in-house review requires deal importance, counterparty history and commercial relationships. These emphases are complementary rather than a direct disagreement: operational visibility supports allocation, while business context informs judgment. DHL’s investment in analysts, data science and IT illustrates the supporting capabilities; the accounts do not quantify forecasting accuracy or returns. On the provider side, the General Legal discussion offers workflow decomposition and bottleneck monitoring as an anecdotal precedent for redesign.

qs.q: [snorts] The really tricky bit is all of the orchestration and the coordination.
qs.a: Ross McNairn — Wordsmith.ai (in-house legal orchestration) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: They're completely business specific concepts, but they impact how you actually go do the legal work and the way that you think about it.
qs.a: E36 - Too Much FOMO: Why I'm Back on the Legal AI Startup Investor Train with Sandstone CEO Nick Fleisher · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Reusable legal data may shift access and control toward clients and business users without eliminating professional judgment.
kps.d: Berrent describes converting lengthy private-market documents into lawyer-verified data for comparisons, trends and outliers. She reports early client appetite for direct access and anticipates less dependence on outside counsel’s knowledge of market terms. How AI Has Tech Companies Pivoting similarly advocates on-demand contract information and describes sales-team self-service creation. Klinger supplies an internal example: Moderna’s regulatory tracking and gap-analysis tool contrasts with previously purchased law-firm monitoring, while an HR GPT standardises documentation without replacing the qualitative conversation. These accounts illustrate changed interfaces and work allocation, not proof that external advice or human checking is unnecessary.

qs.q: So, you know, whatever the answers are, it's been verified by a lawyer.
qs.a: Jen Berrent — Covenant (founder) on structure, conflicts and legal data in private markets · AI-native providers · 2026

qs.q: There's a self-serve that allows, for example, sales teams to create their own contracts.
qs.a: How AI Has Tech Companies Pivoting · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Consolidation creates access-governance and security obligations alongside analytical opportunities.
kps.d: The legal-marketing discussion argues that documents, clients, matters and people have context-dependent relationships shared across marketing, knowledge management and conflicts. Its speaker supports breaking down silos but recommends permissions that reflect circumstances and information walls, including when using Harvey. These are anticipated governance challenges, not reported breaches. Darr’s deployment account supplies a practical constraint: ready data accelerated a model project now used by attorneys and paralegals, but IT faced more complicated security work behind the firewall. Data availability therefore does not establish deployment ease or permission to reuse information for every purpose.

qs.q: And so it's awesome that we're going to start breaking down these silos and putting all this data together, but we have a responsibility once we put it together to make sure that we're honoring that information and treating it the appropriate way.
qs.a: Legal Marketing, AI, Innovation, and Why People Still Come First · Law firms · 2026

qs.q: And so that was one of the quick things that we could take advantage of just because we had the data there and it was ready.
qs.a: Elaine Darr — DHL Supply Chain (VP Legal & Regulatory Affairs) on legal ops, trained models, and market-rate billing enforcement · In-house counsel · 2025

kps.k: Outcome-led measurement requires more than counts of activity, speed or product adoption.
kps.d: McIver recommends dashboards tied to business priorities and external rate benchmarks to interpret internal spending. McNairn distinguishes legal impact from output volume; his interviewer adds that significant risk may justify spending more and moving slower. Haroun similarly favours commercial outcomes over incremental task productivity. The unresolved issue is how to substantiate that value: Wordsmith estimates savings against an assumption-based outsourcing counterfactual; Haroun’s 90% faster deal-closing ambition and claimed ability to cut outside-counsel bills by 20% are not demonstrated results here. His preliminary association between contract language and margins 50 basis points higher may not survive fuller analysis. Saunders’s adoption and retention figures support reported use, not accuracy or improved legal outcomes. Practical measurement must distinguish forecasts, associations, estimated avoided costs and realised benefits.

qs.q: And I think that that’s where you see the biggest shift is the folks that are getting in there and creating dashboards that aren’t just everything thrown up, but ones that are tying into their KPIs that are tying into their business strategies.
qs.a: Data First, Partner Better. Jennifer McIver on Legal Ops Benchmarks, AI Agents, and Pricing Reality Checks · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: You want to be telling the company, "No, this is a good significant enough risk  that we ought to be spending money and and moving slower." Um, so I, you know, that's that's a huge benefit.
qs.a: Ross McNairn — Wordsmith.ai (in-house legal orchestration) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: These curated AI-native legal-provider sources collectively build on the proposition by coupling usable legal data with a broader redesign of service delivery. Berrent directly accepts the data-centred case: lengthy documents become structured, lawyer-verified information that clients can compare, query and use more directly. Walker materially extends that logic from the data layer to the provider’s operating model, arguing that technology should underpin incentives, staffing, workflow engineering and the client interface rather than be added to an incumbent law-firm structure. The common rationale is that transformation requires redesigning how legal information and work move through the service, not merely deploying another tool. There is material internal variation: Berrent focuses on document-to-data conversion, verification and client control of knowledge, while Walker focuses on technology-first organisational architecture, bottleneck monitoring and customer experience without substantially addressing selective data preparation, business-context linkage, permissions or security. Neither account provides measured causal evidence: Berrent describes early-stage product adoption and client appetite, while Walker relies partly on an operational anecdote and commercial thesis. The sources therefore extend rather than contradict the cluster, but they should not be treated as representative of AI-native providers generally.

qs.q: And all of a sudden now I have this complicated you know you know 100page plus document that is a lot of words that has now come into uh you know the format of data that I can graph I can compare I can you know think about I can see trends I can see outliers and that has just been you know sort of magnificent for clients to to start to experience that.
qs.a: Jen Berrent — Covenant (founder) on structure, conflicts and legal data in private markets · AI-native providers · 2026

qs.q: So to structure a company from the ground up with the the with technology as the foundation, layering a legal services uh operation on top of that so that that you know you can actually have the right incentives in place, have the right kind of uh processes and the right kind of people to deliver this next generation of legal services.
qs.a: Ryan Walker — General Legal: The Rise of AI-Native Law Firms and the AmLaw Reshuffle · AI-native providers · 2026

vlens.an: The selected in-house counsel and legal-operations sources accept the principal proposition and materially extend it through concrete implementation accounts. Their shared reasoning is that transformation depends on converting fragmented legal records into operationally useful information: integrating legal and business systems, adding specialist data capability, and embedding outputs in workflows for demand forecasting, staffing, risk analysis, regulatory monitoring and consistent documentation. Darr further develops the proposition’s governance dimension by reporting that ready data accelerated deployment while security and behind-the-firewall implementation remained substantially more complex. Klinger illustrates how structured workflows can improve reliability and user access without displacing qualitative human judgment. Smolik adds an organisational-capability argument: usable data requires dedicated personnel not only to structure it but also to interpret it. Material variation lies in emphasis and evidential strength. Darr focuses on infrastructure, resourcing and security; Klinger on workflow applications and preserving judgment; and Smolik on predictive business advice and specialist roles. Their evidence is mainly qualitative practitioner reporting rather than quantified proof of accuracy, productivity or realised return. Darr and Smolik also describe the same DHL organisational setting, so their accounts should not be treated as independent demonstrations. These curated sources support and develop the proposition, but they do not establish how prevalent these practices are among in-house teams.

qs.q: Um and then on top of that we have spent a lot of time and hiring analysts on our team to actually take all the data that's available in those underlying applications and and pull it together with some of the business applications to have a full suite of reporting.
qs.a: Elaine Darr — DHL Supply Chain (VP Legal & Regulatory Affairs) on legal ops, trained models, and market-rate billing enforcement · In-house counsel · 2025

vlens.an: These selected traditional law-firm sources accept the principal proposition that operational transformation requires usable, connected data and redesigned workflows rather than merely adding AI tools. Their common reasoning is that automation will amplify poor processes and data, while structured document extraction and linked records can create new analytical visibility. Collectively, they materially develop the proposition by specifying how firms should proceed: prioritise high-value cleaning rather than attempt to standardise everything; model documents, clients, matters and people as context-dependent relationships; and introduce granular access controls as information silos are dismantled. There is some internal variation in emphasis. Nuara’s discussion concentrates on workflow decomposition, talent and the productive potential of document data extraction, supported mainly by analogy and a project anecdote. The legal-marketing source focuses more directly on cross-functional information relationships and the governance obligations created by consolidation, including information walls and circumstance-dependent permissions. Neither supplies quantified evidence of operational outcomes, and Nuara gives limited attention to security or access governance. This assessment describes only the curated sources supplied, not traditional law firms generally.

qs.q: if if you start with a messy processes and data, you’re going to amplify that messy process and that messy data rather than clean it up.
qs.a: Flatiron Law Group's Lennie Nuara on Talent-First AI, M&A Workflows, and the Future of Legal Practice · Law firms · 2026

qs.q: And so it's awesome that we're going to start breaking down these silos and putting all this data together, but we have a responsibility once we put it together to make sure that we're honoring that information and treating it the appropriate way.
qs.a: Legal Marketing, AI, Innovation, and Why People Still Come First · Law firms · 2026

vlens.an: The curated legal-tech-vendor sources support the proposition that AI-enabled legal transformation depends on converting fragmented legal records into usable, connected operational information rather than merely deploying another tool. Their common reasoning is that legal data becomes valuable when it is selectively prepared, tied to business demand and context, embedded in workflows, and assessed through business impact rather than activity or adoption alone. There is material variation in emphasis: McIver and Saunders focus on data quality and separating useful information from low-value material; Fleisher and the contract-product speakers emphasise commercial context and business-user access; Haroun connects legal, financial and operational data to specified outcomes while retaining expert judgment; and McNairn goes furthest by treating aggregated legal work as a source of truth for orchestration and ROI measurement. The evidence is chiefly practitioner reasoning, product descriptions and vendor-reported adoption or value claims, not independent proof of causal outcomes. Access controls and security—important qualifications in the proposition—receive little direct treatment in these vendor sources, but that omission does not amount to opposition.

qs.q: Everybody wants those kind of easy button, know, I’m going to use AI and you realize that your data is scattered and your data isn’t the best.
qs.a: Data First, Partner Better. Jennifer McIver on Legal Ops Benchmarks, AI Agents, and Pricing Reality Checks · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: So, you need to aggregate the work, which is our mission really is to become that source of truth for all legal work.
qs.a: Ross McNairn — Wordsmith.ai (in-house legal orchestration) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: This curated market/consultancy/press source supports the proposition’s selective data-preparation approach. Skoghag argues that firms should make their own documents and management systems coherent and reliable, while rejecting the assumption that client-supplied data can meet identical metadata or formatting standards. She therefore supports designing procurement and workflows to tolerate variable inputs rather than waiting for comprehensive standardisation. The main internal variation is between the interviewer’s stronger framing—imposing consistency to enable AI—and Skoghag’s qualified “yes and no”: internal consistency is attainable, but external inputs require flexibility. Her claims are grounded in professional experience, not measured evidence of operational outcomes, and this single curated source cannot establish how prevalent the view is among market analysts, consultancies or the press.

qs.q: How do we structure our own documents and how do we structure our own you know management systems and throughout how do we make that neat coherent and reliable?
qs.a: Emelie Skoghag: How Legal Technologists Transform Law Firms · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: it frankly not realistic that we can require the exact same level of structure works as what we currently have in our mapping systems with metadata etc etc so I think you do need to be mindful when you're both in  procurement and in building workflows later on that you need to have structures in place to allow for that flexibility.
qs.a: Emelie Skoghag: How Legal Technologists Transform Law Firms · Market & press · 2026

elens.an: The 2025 sources collectively accept the proposition and materially develop it with operational examples of deployment. They commonly argue that AI-enabled legal transformation rests on making fragmented legal and business records usable within defined workflows: DHL integrates intake, matter, spend and business data for reporting and staffing; Moderna applies connected information to regulatory gap analysis and standardised HR documentation; McIver and Saunders stress selecting useful information from scattered or low-value data; and the contract source extends this logic to business-user access and self-service. Material variation concerns emphasis rather than direction. Darr focuses on specialist analysts, production deployment and security complexity; Smolik on interpretation and risk anticipation; McIver on KPI-linked, selective preparation; Klinger on preserving qualitative human judgment; and Saunders on vendor-reported adoption and retention. The evidence remains chiefly practitioner testimony and product description: uptake, implementation and anticipated value are better supported than accuracy, causal operational gains or realised business outcomes. Access controls receive little attention outside Darr’s security account. Because this is a curated selection, the alignment shows how these sources relate to the proposition, not how prevalent these views were in 2025.

qs.q: Um and then on top of that we have spent a lot of time and hiring analysts on our team to actually take all the data that's available in those underlying applications and and pull it together with some of the business applications to have a full suite of reporting.
qs.a: Elaine Darr — DHL Supply Chain (VP Legal & Regulatory Affairs) on legal ops, trained models, and market-rate billing enforcement · In-house counsel · 2025

qs.q: And all the data security elements from our IT perspective is much more complicated because they have to worry about so much more, right?
qs.a: Elaine Darr — DHL Supply Chain (VP Legal & Regulatory Affairs) on legal ops, trained models, and market-rate billing enforcement · In-house counsel · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition that legal transformation depends on usable, connected data and redesigned workflows rather than merely deploying new tools, and they materially extend it into a more developed operating model. Common reasons include the need to avoid amplifying poor data and processes, prepare data selectively, accommodate irregular client inputs, connect legal work to commercial context, and aggregate workload so value can be measured by business impact rather than activity. They further develop the proposition through lawyer verification of extracted data, context-sensitive permissions and information walls, client access to reusable legal knowledge, and orchestration of legal demand. Material variation concerns emphasis rather than broad rejection: some sources focus on data preparation and governance; others on client control, in-house business context or outcome measurement. The General Legal discussion redirects toward a technology-first legal-services model and modern client interface without substantially addressing connected records or governance. Claims of operational and financial benefit are mostly practitioner accounts, product descriptions, preliminary associations or forecasts—not measured causal evidence—and the sources themselves sometimes acknowledge imperfect inputs, early-stage adoption and uncertain ROI. Because this is a curated set, these positions should not be treated as representative of all 2026 participants or as evidence of prevalence.
